articles.title: Utilizing digital ethnography techniques to expand walkthrough method using participant-generated media
articles.authors: Renee Mitson
articles.abstract: Walkthrough has found modern application as a methodology in user experience scholarship and practice to allow researchers to qualitatively “walk,” step-by-step, through a digital interface and examine functions, communication, implications, and usability. Simultaneously, existing users of digital platforms have begun creating media of themselves walking through properties for the benefit of their digital communities, leading to the rise of user-generated walkthroughs. These user-generated walkthroughs share user experience, provide situated expertise, and circulate knowledge within digital communities. Despite this growth, walkthrough methodology has largely developed within UX and human–computer interaction contexts and lacks deeper integration with social scientific and ethnographic priorities. User-generated walkthroughs in communication research present a unique opportunity to bridge these traditions by bringing the rigor and epistemological commitments of digital ethnography into conversation with walkthrough practice. In doing so, participant-generated walkthroughs center participant knowledge, positioning users as active interpreters who signal what is meaningful in digital environments. This manuscript proposes theoretical and methodological directions for future participant-generated walkthrough research, arguing that digital ethnographic considerations provide the necessary structure for more rigorous and socially grounded applications of the Walkthrough method, while also opening new possibilities for qualitative and computational inquiry in digital spaces.

articles.title: Living a dating life, rewriting romantic scripts: Young women’s dating diaries and popular feminism on Xiaohongshu
articles.authors: Yan Tan, Shih-Diing Liu
articles.abstract: This article examines how young women narrate their dating experiences on Xiaohongshu, a Chinese social media platform centered on lifestyle blogging, to explore the platformization of cultural production and emerging feminist sensibilities around romance. Drawing on textual analysis and interviews, the article reveals that dating diaries constitute a unique cultural genre that foregrounds female-centered romantic narratives, offering an alternative to hegemonic patriarchal norms. Although these narratives emphasize female autonomy and agency, they are shaped by Xiaohongshu’s cultural scripts, resulting in individualized, aestheticized, and commercialized forms of storytelling that undercut their feminist potential. We argue that these practices exemplify a localized form of popular feminism in China, marked by its ambivalence as it negotiates visibility, commodification, and political sensitivity within a commercialized and regulated digital media ecosystem.

articles.title: Global reach, local constraints: senior professionals on the streamers’ impact on creative power, autonomy, and authorship in the Flemish audiovisual industry
articles.authors: Jens Van Landschoot, Daniel Biltereyst
articles.abstract: Streaming platforms have transformed opportunities for European filmmakers, providing global reach and essential additional funding. However, these platforms also challenge notions of creative autonomy and authorship. Insights derived from thirteen in-depth interviews with senior industry professionals from the Flemish film and audiovisual market – primarily filmmakers, producers, and other professional stakeholders – reveal the complexities of this evolving creative landscape. This offers deeper insights into the interrelated challenges of creative freedom and collaboration with streamers. Three key perspectives emerge. First, almost all interviewed professionals acknowledge streaming platforms’ importance regarding additional financing. Over the last decade, these have increasingly become important as additional investors in an ecosystem increasingly challenged by a strained economic environment. Second, stakeholders highlight concerns over creative control when working with streamers. Although these platforms offer vital resources, they often impose rigid guidelines to cater to algorithm-driven global audiences, limiting filmmakers’ autonomy and control over final cuts. The third perspective suggests a convergence of cinema, streaming formats, and creative practices. Many directors are drawn to the series format for its potential for extended storytelling and its capability to sustain audiences’ attention for longer periods. This interplay creates new creative opportunities but also blurs the lines between traditional cinematic and serialized narratives and content, while simultaneously fostering homogenization processes.

articles.title: Platformed nostalgia: Techlash and the commercialisation of historical social media nostalgia on Tumblr
articles.authors: Briony Hannell
articles.abstract: This article conceptualises platformed nostalgia as a social media platform branding strategy that commodifies historical social media nostalgia to (re)gain social acceptance and legitimacy in response to popular techlash towards contemporary social media platforms. Drawing on a critical discourse analysis of 193 marketing and platform communication documents authored by and/or related to Tumblr under Automattic’s ownership (2019-), it argues that platformed nostalgia is cultivated through platform branding and communication strategies that instrumentalise users’ assumed nostalgic attachments to an imagined utopic past of early social media alongside normative platform values of transparency, democracy, and public good. The findings reveal that, in Tumblr’s case, the latter are invoked to position the platform as a nostalgic foil to real or imagined irresponsible or less responsible corporate social media platforms of the present, such as X (formerly Twitter). The analysis therefore explores how popular forms of historical social media nostalgia emerging from discontentment with and critique of the technocultural present are vulnerable to commercial co-optation by social media platforms.

articles.title: Drawing boundaries: How creative practitioners navigate precarity in AI-embedded creative work
articles.authors: Jie Huang, Graham Hitchen, Safak Dogan
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) continues to grow within creative industries, existing research has examined its implications for creative labour. However, much of this work emphasises AI’s impact on efficiency gains or creativity, offering limited insight into how practitioners adopt AI tools and negotiate human-AI boundaries in practical contexts under conditions of creative precarity. To bridge the gaps, this study applies boundary work theory to examine how creative practitioners redefine what remains distinctly human in AI-mediated creative production. Based on 21 interviews with practitioners in the UK film, gaming and live performance sectors, findings show that, in creative work, boundaries between human and AI systems are neither predefined nor passively adjusted to, but are actively shaped, expanded, and maintained in real-world settings. We argue that the adoption of AI is not a simple technical adjustment but a process through which professional value and the dynamic of creative work are reconsidered and re-constituted. Practitioners intentionally engage in boundary activities to navigate the unstable work environment associated with AI integration, enabling them to defend the role of creator. Theoretically, this study demonstrates the explanatory power of boundary work theory for understanding AI-embedded creative production and identifies that boundaries are not drawn by practitioners alone but through the interplay of technological capacities, project demands, and the legal environment. Practically, it suggests the need to redesign creative workflows and refresh professional skill sets to maintain meaningful human control while also facilitating efficient human-AI collaboration.

articles.title: Hydraen narrative: Conceptualising inclusive and resistant fiction
articles.authors: R. Lyle Skains
articles.abstract: Hélène Cixous reclaims the monstrous figure of the Medusa in l’écriture feminine . Discourse on feminist writing has widened to be more inclusive, though we do not yet have corresponding conceptualisation for “writing from without” that encapsulates marginalised authors and subversive texts as eloquently as Cixous does that of the feminine. This paper, arising from practice-based research in writing the hypernovel Seven Sisters Unmet , posits “Hydraen narrative” to refer to the depth and breadth of narratives written from outside and resisting the homogenising effects of dominant culture. Hydraen narratives are those that proliferate under suppression and reclaim demonised creative excess through previously termed “feminist” structures, styles, and/or content: polyvocality, lack of closure, repetition, ontological metelepsis, unnatural narrative techniques, embodiment, intra- and intertextuality, questions of family versus self, and explorations of sexuality and gender. Hydraen narrative using digital interfaces galvanises the dialectical, participatory relationship between creator and audience that can lead to social change and restored (and restorative) power.

articles.title: Finding Love in the Black Box: Algorithm Awareness on Dating Apps
articles.authors: Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans
articles.abstract: Most dating apps use algorithms to match users to one another, but are not fully transparent about how their recommender systems work. In turn, users have varying degrees of awareness of matching algorithms. Unfortunately, little is known about how awareness of algorithmic functioning relates to online dating. This research examined the relationship between algorithm awareness, trust in algorithms, and satisfaction with the quality of matches. A survey was conducted among 500 users of the Dutch dating app Breeze, presented to respondents within the app itself. Relationships were estimated with structural equation modeling. Higher algorithm awareness was associated with more trust in algorithms, which positively related to satisfaction with the quality of matches. This mediated association between awareness and satisfaction with matches suggested that awareness of matching algorithms is associated with better outcomes of dating app use. This research contributes to the limited literature on human–algorithm interaction on dating apps. Overall, the results suggest that algorithm awareness may be a relevant part of the online dating experience.

articles.title: A genealogy of conceptual confusion: Epistemological fault lines across media-ritual concepts
articles.authors: Hung-Yen Hsu
articles.abstract: Research on media–ritual intersections deploys seven concepts: media events, media rituals, mediatized rituals, media ritualization, ritual mediatization, ritual media, and ritualized media. Their overlap generates unmarked substitution between analytically divergent registers. The slippage is a structural consequence of three epistemological tributaries (Durkheimian social theory, Carey's ritual view, and mediatization theory), each foregrounding a different dimension of the same phenomena. Genealogical analysis diagnoses four confusions: process conflated with product, unmarked shifting among power paradigms, materiality–practice divergence, and directional inversion. Three fault lines (integration vs. domination, process vs. structure, exceptional vs. everyday) constitute a meta-theoretical framework. The article advances positioned conceptual deployment: researchers specify their coordinates along all three dimensions. The seven concepts serve as a diagnostic case: concept use in communication research presupposes epistemological commitments, marked or not. An under-theorized intersection, mediatized ritualization, is advanced as a provisional theoretical proposition about how platform architectures may reshape ritualized media practice.

articles.title: He's Just a Pixel Guy: How U.S. Players Experience Otome Games
articles.authors: Elena Yifei Zhao, Nicholas D. Bowman
articles.abstract: Otome games—romantic simulation games centered on relationships between a female player and male non-player characters (NPCs)—have grown into a global phenomenon, yet research on why players find them entertaining remains largely rooted in the Asian cultural context. This study replicates prior work on Chinese players with 131 U.S. otome players, testing whether perceived reciprocity, romantic closeness, hedonic enjoyment, and eudaimonic appreciation are positively associated. H2 and H3 were supported: romantic closeness was positively associated with both hedonic enjoyment (β = .47) and eudaimonic appreciation (β = .71), suggesting that emotional connection with NPCs is a culturally stable correlate of entertainment outcomes. H1, however, was not supported: perceived reciprocity showed no appreciable association with romantic closeness (β = .07, p ∼ .512). We attribute this failure to two factors. First, cultural stigma surrounding otome gaming in the U.S. context may have suppressed the strength of players’ self-reported relational experiences, pulling scores toward neutral. Second, our sample shows that many U.S. players approached the game through the avatar, treating the on-screen protagonist as a distinct character whose romance they observed rather than experienced. These findings suggest that perceived reciprocity is not a universal antecedent of romantic closeness, while romantic closeness itself remains a culturally stable driver of entertainment outcomes.

articles.title: From prompt to profession: how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability through skill development
articles.authors: Bahar Javadi Khasraghi, Qiuli Su, Hanieh Javadi Khasraghi
articles.abstract: Purpose The proliferation of generative AI tools like ChatGPT is transforming higher education, yet evidence of their impact on students' career readiness remains limited. Existing studies often rely on localized samples and emphasize usage frequency over underlying mechanisms. This study investigates how ChatGPT usage relates to students' perceived employability, focusing on perceived proficiency (e.g. writing, communication) and analytical skills (e.g. critical thinking, problem-solving) as mediators. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Self-Perception Theory and Human Capital Theory, with the Technology Acceptance Model providing a conceptual starting point for understanding technology engagement, we use structural equation modeling (SEM) to analyze survey data from 21,716 students across 100 countries, examining associations among ChatGPT use, perceived proficiency and analytical skill development, and perceived employability, with mediation through the two skills. Findings ChatGPT use is positively associated with both skill domains; however, only perceived proficiency is significantly associated with perceived employability. The indirect effect via proficiency is significant, whereas the indirect effect via analytical skills is not, and the direct path from ChatGPT use to employability is nonsignificant, consistent with a full-mediation model. Multi-group analyses indicate stronger effects for students from low- and lower-middle-income countries and for female students, with no substantive differences by field of study. Originality/value This study provides large-scale, theory-driven evidence linking ChatGPT use to perceived skill development and employability. These findings suggest that structured, critical engagement with AI tools may support skill development without displacing deeper learning. It offers critical insights for higher education policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era.

articles.title: Predicting participation and expenditure on distinct gambling-like mechanics: financial engagement, selective problem gambling effects and a gaming disorder null
articles.authors: Topias Mattinen, Joseph Macey, Juho Hamari
articles.abstract: Purpose Quantitative work on gambling-like mechanics (GLMs) in video games has largely treated them as a uniform category, overlooking differences in reward structure and similarity to traditional gambling. This study examines predictors of expenditure across three disaggregated GLM categories – cosmetic loot boxes (CLB), game-affecting loot boxes (GALB) and other in-game gambling-like content (OGLC). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected via an online survey of adult gamers (N = 587). Three model sets used the same gaming engagement and problem behavior indicators as predictors, each comprising a two-part approach: binary logistic regression on the full sample to predict purchase participation, and OLS linear regression among purchasers to predict expenditure amounts. Findings Financial engagement – expenditure on non-random free-to-play content and battle passes – emerged as the dominant predictor class; gaming frequency and gaming disorder were null throughout. Problem gambling severity predicted participation selectively – most strongly for OGLC – but predicted expenditure amounts in no category. Predictor patterns dissociated between participation and amount decisions in ways aggregated or uniform analytic approaches would have obscured. Practical implications Increased focus should be given to paid game mechanics that closely mimic the visual and esthetic presentation of traditional gambling formats. Engagement systems such as battle passes should be carefully assessed for their association with increased expenditure on GLMs. Attention should be paid to the risks related to purchase entry into GLMs, rather than to expenditure amounts alone. Originality/value This study is among the first to apply a disaggregated GLM taxonomy empirically and to model participation and expenditure amount as distinct outcomes.

articles.title: Replenishing resources with enterprise social media (ESM): overload-moderated effects on work-life balance, exhaustion, and turnover
articles.authors: Murad Moqbel, Mohamed Hédi Charki, Amr Soror
articles.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the double-edged impact of Enterprise social media (ESM) use on employee well-being through Conservation of Resources (COR) theory. We examine how work- and nonwork-related ESM use affects work exhaustion and turnover intention via work–life balance (WLB), and how these effects are contingent on perceived work overload. Design/methodology/approach A survey was administered to professionals at a major IT corporation in the Midwestern United States. Data from 276 employees were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings Only nonwork-related ESM use directly promotes WLB. Both work-related and nonwork-related ESM use enhances WLB for employees experiencing high perceived work overload. WLB negatively affects work exhaustion and turnover intention, and work exhaustion positively predicts turnover intention. Perceived work overload is a critical boundary condition shaping the impact of ESM use. Research limitations/implications Because this sample was drawn from a single organization, future research should extend these findings longitudinally and test other ESM-driven spillovers, such as effects on family life. Managers should replace blanket ESM policies with workload-differentiated strategies, encouraging ESM use as a coping resource under high demand while fostering psychologically safe connectivity norms. Originality/value The study offers a contingency-based perspective that reconciles apparent contradictions in ESM literature, moving beyond asking whether ESM has an impact to explaining how and when its effects manifest. A key theoretical contribution is the identification of perceived work overload as a factor that can transform ESM use from a potential drain on resources into a vital coping tool for employee well-being.

articles.title: More, shorter, newer? How monetization reshapes creator strategy on YouTube Shorts
articles.authors: Soonjae Kwon, Kitae Kim, Sung-Hyuk Park
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines the causal impact of YouTube Shorts' ad-revenue sharing policy on creator production strategies in the short-form video creator economy. Design/methodology/approach Using 36,507 videos from 342 top global channels, we employ a regression discontinuity in time design. Computer vision techniques measure four attributes of each creator's production strategy: output volume, video length, editing pace, and content novelty. Findings The policy drove an immediate reduction in video length without expanding output volume, consistent with substitution toward cheaper per-unit configurations rather than output scaling. Entertainment creators shortened their videos most sharply, while informative creators slowed their editing pace to preserve comprehension. Long-type creators pursued per-unit cost reduction, while short-type creators invested in content novelty. Research limitations/implications The sample covers top-tier global channels, so emerging creators may respond differently. The findings show that the quantity-expansion result from low-marginal-cost user-generated content settings does not extend to high-marginal-cost production, where incentives reallocate effort within existing output rather than expand it. Practical implications A uniform monetization policy does not produce uniform outcomes. Incentive design should anticipate that creators adjust different production attributes depending on their content goals and capabilities. Originality/value This study provides causal evidence that performance-contingent monetization reshapes production strategy in a high-cost video production context and that one platform-wide policy generates different responses across creator types.

articles.title: IT professionals' alumni networks and firm innovation: the role of informal connections in dynamic environments
articles.authors: Binger Lin, Chunmian Ge, Junhui Jiang, Yichao Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose We aim to address a critical organizational challenge – how firms can leverage informal networks to enhance innovation in increasingly dynamic environments. Alumni networks connect IT professionals and support knowledge exchange across geographical and organizational boundaries, facilitating innovation through distributed collaboration. However, prior studies have inadequately examined whether and how alumni networks help IT professionals overcome boundary barriers and contribute to firm innovation. Our study fills this gap and offers practical implications for management policies. Design/methodology/approach Using data from a large online professional social networking platform, we construct alumni networks of IT professionals and use linear regression and Poisson models to examine their impact on firm innovation. This study also conducts several robustness tests, including reconstructing the alumni networks, adopting alternative centrality measures, applying different thresholds to identify high-centrality IT professionals and using lagged independent variables. Findings We find that firms with more IT professionals occupying central positions in the alumni network exhibit stronger innovation performance. Furthermore, this positive relationship is strengthened in conditions of high technological and market dynamism, highlighting the value of informal networks in driving innovation in dynamic environments. Originality/value The positive effect of IT professionals' alumni networks on firm innovation extends the understanding of informal networks by highlighting their significance in facilitating information access and integration across organizational boundaries. We further illustrate how the impact of alumni networks varies with environmental dynamism, offering practical insights into how firms can strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity in response to environmental uncertainty.

articles.title: The sequential replicant effect in interpersonal sincerity: evidence from AI-mediated apology and gratitude
articles.authors: Bolin Cao, Zhenming Li
articles.abstract: Sincerity, a core interpersonal value that mobilizes emotional resources, faces distinct challenges in AI-mediated interpersonal contexts. Extending the Replicant Effect from informational trust to interpersonal sincerity, this study examines how AIMC awareness and AI involvement cues shape sincerity judgments and subsequent relational responses. Drawing on two pre-registered, two-round studies in apology (N = 546) and gratitude (N = 561) scenarios, we found that AI involvement cues reliably reduced perceived sincerity. Primed AIMC awareness showed a more sequential influence on later no-cue evaluations through AIMC suspicion. High-ambiguity AI cues produced sequential effects only in the gratitude context. These findings suggest that hybrid human-AI authorship may reshape how interpersonal sincerity is inferred and validated, while also showing that the effects of AI cues and AIMC awareness depend on cue clarity and relational context.

articles.title: It Must Have Been Love (But It's Over Now): Thematic Changes in Popular U.S. Song Lyrics Across 4+ Decades
articles.authors: Janet B. Ruscher, Katherine B. Carnelley
articles.abstract: Over time, U.S. marriage rates have decreased, as people increasingly expect romantic relationships to satisfy high-level needs. Concurrently, interest in sexualized relationships (e.g., hook-ups; consensual nonmonogamy) has increased. Reflecting these patterns over time, song lyrics may become less about prototypical romantic love and more about noncommitted sexual relationships. Using the Meaning Extraction module in LIWC-22, four independent content themes were pulled from the top 25 songs of the Billboard Hot 100 from 1980 to 2024 ( N = 1,129). Themes were correlated with chart year and LIWC linguistic categories. Lyrics high on a Fall in (or out of) Love theme (content words like love, heart, break ) became less common and used past and future tense. In contrast, lyrics high on a Contact theme (e.g., talk, stop, call) became more common, more sexualized (sexual and swear words), and avoided future tense. The advantage of Meaning Extraction for testing hypotheses about language with large data is discussed.

articles.title: A Framework for Classifying Uncertainties in AI-Driven Newsrooms
articles.authors: Luna Paladino, Paula Chimenti, André Fonseca
articles.abstract: This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is adopted and integrated into the newsroom of a major Brazilian media organization—Globo. While AI deployment in journalism has expanded globally, the experiences lived by journalists in contexts that are not Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic remain underexplored. Combining in-depth interviews, internal documents, organizational presentations, public materials, and direct observation within a qualitative case study, this study analyzes how GAI is reshaping newsroom practices, routines, and professional identities. It introduces a framework for classifying uncertainties in AI-driven newsrooms, a type II theory, which is designed to describe, classify, and organize the main forms of uncertainty faced by journalists when interacting with GAI systems, and then structure these uncertainties into three analytical levels—macro (ecosystem), meso (organization), and micro (identity)—while pairing each level with its associated coping strategies. Given its single-case basis, the framework is presented as a possible framework whose analytical categories require further empirical application before broader validation.

articles.title: Methods Hub: A Community-Driven, Interactive Platform for Open-Source Computational Tools and Tutorials
articles.authors: Christina Viehmann, Johannes Kiesel, Arnim Bleier, Chung-hong Chan, Po-Chun Chang, Raniere Gaia Costa da Silva, Ahrabhi Kathirgamalingam, Taimoor Khan, Stephan Linzbach, Fakhri Momeni, Felix Münch, Ran Yu, Stefan Dietze, Claudia Wagner
articles.abstract: As computational methods become increasingly central to social science research, there is a growing demand for research software infrastructures that are sustainable, grounded in principles of open science, and embedded in the community. In response, we are introducing the Methods Hub as an open-source, community-driven collection of computational tools designed to support social science research in solving complex data-related tasks. The Methods Hub integrates three complementary components: First, quality-curated content, including computational methods and accompanying tutorials, which are specifically presented from a social science research perspective. Second, the methods and tutorials are hosted on a web portal enabling researchers to discover, apply, learn, and publish computational methods. Third, interactive, browser-based execution backends allow users to directly run, test, and adapt the code of methods and tutorials. These components are guided by a set of core principles: a long-term infrastructure perspective, reproducibility requirements, and a focus on community. The Methods Hub builds a long-term infrastructure that extends beyond the scope of single projects. Further, reproducibility functions as a quality assurance measure while advancing the practices of open science. Finally, the Methods Hub is built on public, community-based submissions by treating research software as citable academic output and providing visibility, accessibility, and formal recognition. We are also broadening the community by fostering learning and ease of access. Looking ahead, the Methods Hub is exploring the potential of AI as both a research tool and to further strengthen the infrastructure, while maintaining transparency, reproducibility, and quality standards for computational social science research.

articles.title: Social Media “Image Operations” During the Tigray War (2020–2022)
articles.authors: Matti Pohjonen, Amanuel Tesfaye Kebede
articles.abstract: This article examines the use of social media images during the Tigray War (2020–2022), one of the world’s deadliest armed conflicts of the 21st century. Drawing on a corpus of 92.9 million tweets and over 500,000 images shared on Twitter, we analyse what types of images were shared by the opposing sides of the conflict and what specific functions these images served in antagonistic information campaigns. The article shows how images were used not only to amplify the opposing strategic narratives about war but also to shape the emotional or affective registers related to it. The pro-Tigray campaign relied on the heavy use of emotive images of casualties as well as images of material destruction, which, combined with the use of infographics, collectively conveyed victimhood with the goal of putting pressure on the Ethiopian government and its allies. The pro-government side, in turn, relied more on images that tried to evoke patriotism and resistance in the audience, organise protests, as well as represent a stance of anti-colonial defiance against international pressure. The article contributes to the growing literature on digital media in contemporary conflicts by proposing a novel research framework and methodology and providing original empirical findings on an understudied dimension of contemporary conflicts.

articles.title: Proxies in Print: Strategic Narratives of the Sudan Conflict in Digital Media
articles.authors: Téwodros W. Workneh
articles.abstract: The Sudanese civil war exemplifies how contemporary proxy conflicts are fiercely contested within digital information ecologies. Utilizing strategic narrative theory, this study examines the structural weaponization of transnational journalism to construct the geopolitical ontology of state collapse. An interpretive analysis of 402 English-language articles from Qatar’s <em>Al Jazeera English</em>, the UAE’s <em>The National</em>, and the US’s <em>The New York Times</em> reveals significant divergences in narrative projection. <em>The New York Times </em>frames the crisis through a “global instability” index, actively legitimizing US-led diplomatic intervention. <em>Al Jazeera English </em>deploys an identity narrative of “state victimhood” to delegitimize rival paramilitaries and subtextually indict competing Gulf patrons. In stark contrast, <em>The National</em> exercises “humanitarian obfuscation,” actively depoliticizing the disaster to shield Emirati proxy interventions from international scrutiny. These findings demonstrate that democratic and authoritarian regimes alike systematically co-opt digital news platforms as soft power arsenals to dictate the geopolitical imaginaries of the Global South.

articles.title: The Metajournalistic Discourse and the Sociopolitical Construction of AI Risk in Chinese Journalism
articles.authors: Youyi Wei
articles.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into journalism has improved production efficiency but raised concerns about its potential to compromise content quality and undermine journalists’ professional capacity. These tensions are particularly pronounced in China, where AI deployment in journalism intersects with state-led advocacy and professional authority. Drawing on metajournalistic discourse and taking a sociopolitical perspective, I examine how journalistic discourse frames and responds to AI risks in structurally constrained contexts. I conducted a textual analysis of 102 articles published between 2022 and 2025 by Chinese journalists affiliated with institutional media. These articles narrate journalists’ perceptions of, or working experiences with, AI. AI risks are discursively framed at three levels: content quality, mainstream values, and professional subjectivity. Journalistic discourse constructs an asymmetrical attribution of these risks, assigning responsibility primarily to opaque AI systems, technology companies, and individual journalists positioned as “risk filters,” while largely overlooking the responsibilities of media organizations and the state. Political intervention, institutional hierarchy, and professional commitments shape adaptive boundary work that aligns with state-led AI advocacy while establishing boundaries by limiting AI capability in journalistic work. This study provides an empirical account of how journalists negotiate AI risks and professional autonomy amid advanced AI development and state-sanctioned boundaries, extending Western-centric and Global South research.

articles.title: FOMO in Sub-Saharan African AI Hype: The Quest for a Decolonized AI Adoption Framework
articles.authors: Danford Zirugo, Bruce Mutsvairo
articles.abstract: Based on an abductive analysis of 54 opinion, editorial, and analytical articles published between 2019 and 2025 in nine English-speaking Sub-Saharan African countries, this study examines negotiation of the place of AI within journalism. Conceptualizing AI hype as a form of metajournalistic discourse, the study finds that discussions about AI in journalism in Sub-Saharan Africa are driven by a fear of missing out and a call for a decolonial approach to the technology’s adoption in a way sensitive to the region’s context.

articles.title: Praise, rent, and the platform: Substack and the enclosure of blog culture
articles.authors: Will Riley
articles.abstract: This article situates Substack within the platformisation of blogging and the enclosure of cultural production within proprietary infrastructures. Tracing the genealogy of blogging as a decentralised practice that carried within it the seeds of citizen journalism and informal intellectual life, I argue that Substack does not restore an apparently lost cultural practice but renegotiates and interpolates blogging into a platformised logic. Framed as a return to independent, writer-led publishing, Substack instead, as I argue, renders free-labour interaction as a source of rent. I analyse the rhetoric and revolving discourse around Substack’s internal curatorial project, ‘The Substack Post’. Drawing on Jodi Dean’s account of blogs as displaced mediators alongside theories of digital labour and platform capitalism, and approaching Substack as a simultaneously platformised and infrastructuralised formation, I argue that praise operates as a platform-specific form of commodity fetishism, animating the platform while obscuring the labour relations that sustain it.

articles.title: Platformed affective withdrawal: Quiet quitting and the refusal of gendered emotional labour on TikTok
articles.authors: Aybüke Büyükkağnıcı
articles.abstract: This article examines #quietquitting on TikTok as a platform-mediated articulation of gendered affective withdrawal. While organisational research interprets quiet quitting as reduced discretionary effort or declining work engagement, this study examines how quiet quitting is articulated as a digitally circulated refusal of feminised emotional labour. Drawing on feminist theories of affective labour and critical platform studies, the analysis explores how workers renegotiate expectations of emotional availability within algorithmically structured visibility regimes. The study is based on a qualitative-dominant mixed-methods analysis of 586 TikTok videos shared under #quietquitting between 2020 and 2026. Combining thematic discourse analysis with descriptive engagement indicators, the findings show that creators frequently frame quiet quitting as a refusal of unpaid relational mediation, emotional management, and workplace care. The article introduces the concept of platformed affective withdrawal to explain how narratives of workplace disengagement circulate through algorithmic visibility systems that amplify and individualise gendered labour inequalities.

articles.title: A Job Demands-Resources Perspective on Science Communication: How Public Engagement Shapes Scientist Communicators’ Well-Being
articles.authors: Anthony Dudo, Josh T. L. Anderson
articles.abstract: Scientists are increasingly expected to engage public audiences, yet little is known about how this work shapes their well-being. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with scientist communicators and guided by the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, this study examines demands and resources scientists associate with public communication. Findings reveal that demands including time pressure, harassment, reputational risk, and unsupportive institutional practices substantially outweigh available resources, including training and institutional support. Evidence of burnout and disengagement suggests these conditions are unsustainable. We discuss implications for science communication infrastructure, pedagogy, and the utility of the JD-R model as an organizing framework for this inquiry.

articles.title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
articles.authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler-Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, Sara B. Hobolt, Claes de Vreese
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) dramatically lowers the costs of creating high-quality, realistic images, allowing a wider range of actors to create and distribute such content on, for instance, social media. A core concern is that easy-to-use generative AI tools can be misused for manipulation through misinformation and microtargeted persuasive material. However, we still need more contextual nuance to a fundamental question: To what degree can people discern photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images? In a preregistered survey experiment, we find that, on average, people are not substantially better than chance at discerning AI-generated images from authentic images, regardless of the context of the image. While younger people, highly analytical-thinking individuals, and experienced users of generative AI have better discernment abilities, no demographic group other than young individuals (<25) performs substantially better than chance. Contrary to our expectation, we do not find that people’s confidence in their discernment abilities varies depending on the context of the image. As generative AI technology likely advances and the realism of AI-generated images continues to improve, these findings are concerning, as people already struggle to discern between AI-generated and authentic images, even in an experiment where they have been primed and are assessing images of relatively low quality.

articles.title: Digital Archives of Feelings: Rethinking cultural memory and humanistic spirit through visual design
articles.authors: Xianwen Liang, Zhili Yun, Endale Tadesse, Jiang Diankun
articles.abstract: This article argues that as digitalisation and artificial intelligence become increasingly embedded in design practice, the preservation of cultural memory is shifting from physical spaces to digital environments structured by data and algorithms. While these technological transformations open up new possibilities for design methods and the transmission of cultural memory, they also introduce challenges: algorithm-driven rationality risks reducing the depth of human emotions and homogenising diverse cultural memories. Drawing on the theory of Archives of Feelings and visual culture studies, and adopting the concept of historical empathy proposed as a framework, this study analyses three key dimensions of cultural memory as mediated through visual design: social collective memory, marginalised group memory and human–AI collaborative memory. It further explores how visual design can negotiate between technological rationality and humanistic care, ensuring that Digital Archives of Feelings sustain diverse cultural memories while preserving emotional depth.

articles.title: Representation of ethnic minorities: visual rhetoric on the covers of Nationality Pictorial (1955–2024)
articles.authors: Yuan Zhang, Xinrui Li
articles.abstract: This article examines the visual representation of ethnic minorities on the covers of Nationality Pictorial (1955–2024), a state-level pictorial in China devoted to minority affairs. Drawing on a longitudinal dataset of 735 covers and a multimodal discourse analysis framework, the study analyzes how visual rhetoric mediates the relationship between ethnic identity, political ideology and market imperatives across three historical periods. The findings reveal a clear shift in representational strategies: from collectivist imagery emphasising socialist unity during the early years of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), to highly politicised symbolism during the Cultural Revolution, and finally to individualised, aestheticised, and commodified portrayals in the reform and opening-up period. Across these phases, cover images employ recurring rhetorical devices to align ethnic representation with shifting state–market agendas. The study argues that Nationality Pictorial covers were not neutral reflections of minority life, but rather state-mediated constructions that stabilised ideological narratives and shaped collective memory. By demonstrating how visual codes adapt to political and economic change, the research advances debates on visual rhetoric, media ideology and the politics of multicultural representation.
